opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most interesting open design questions right now. The basic idea is simple: if a model generates value, the people whose data made it good should share in that value, not just the company that trained it. Doing that well is much harder than it sounds.

First, not all data is equal. Dumping a million scraped web pages into a training set isn't the same as a domain expert writing high-quality reasoning traces, or someone labeling edge cases where the model is failing. So the reward shouldn't scale with volume. It should reflect marginal contribution: how much did this data actually improve the model on things people care about? That pushes you toward evaluation-driven attribution. You run benchmarks, maybe ablations or influence-function-style estimates, and allocate tokens based on measured impact. None of these methods are perfect, but they're much better than paying per byte, which just invites spam.

Second, timing matters. If you pay everything up front, contributors have no stake in whether the model succeeds. Model-specific tokens are nice because they align incentives. If the model gets used, if inference demand grows, if it gets fine-tuned into downstream products, the token captures some of that value and contributors benefit over time. It's closer to equity in the model than a one-time bounty.

Third, you need protection against gaming. As soon as there's money attached, people will submit synthetic garbage, near-duplicates, or even poisoned data. So you need verification: reputation, staking, where you put something at risk when you contribute and lose it if your data is found to be low quality or adversarial, and some community or validator process reviewing contributions. Crypto-economic mechanisms are pretty good at this kind of thing when designed carefully.

Finally, there's the user-owned AI side, which I care a lot about. Contributors should keep some control: knowing how their data is used, opting out of future versions, and having governance rights over where the model goes. The token is the economic layer, but it can also be a governance layer, so the people who built the model collectively have a say in it rather than it being owned by a single entity.

So my short answer: reward measured marginal impact, tie rewards to the model's ongoing success, make contributors put skin in the game to prevent abuse, and give them real ownership, not just a payout. We're still early, and a lot of this needs experimentation, but I think it's the direction things have to go if we want AI that's actually aligned with the people who make it possible.

r001.rationale: It proposes model-specific tokens for contributors and says rewards should reflect how much their data improves the model.

r002.rationale: It says tokens can capture value as model use grows and contributors can benefit over time, but does not clearly propose distributing the model’s revenue to token holders throughout its lifetime.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we've been thinking about a lot at NEAR, and I think it really comes down to the attribution problem. Right now, if you contribute data to a model, you give it away and you're done. There's no ongoing relationship between the value you created and the value the model generates. So the idea with a model-specific token is that the token essentially represents a share of that model's future economic output.

The way I'd frame it is: when a model gets trained, everyone who contributed data, or compute, or even evaluation and feedback, gets allocated tokens proportional to their contribution. And then every time the model is used, when someone pays for inference, a portion of that revenue flows back to token holders. So you're not just getting a one-time payment, you're getting a continuous stream as long as the model is useful.

Now, the hard part is figuring out what "proportional" means. You can't just count bytes. A thousand examples of high-quality, rare domain data might be worth way more than a million scraped web pages. So you need some mechanism to measure marginal contribution. There's work on things like data Shapley values, where you basically ask how much does model performance change if you remove this data, and that gives you a principled way to assign credit. It's expensive to compute exactly, but there are approximations that work reasonably well.

The other piece that matters to me is that this should be verifiable and transparent. If I contribute data and I'm told I'll get a certain share, I should be able to check that the training actually happened the way it was described and that the revenue split is honest. That's where blockchain actually makes sense, not as a buzzword, but because you want the accounting to be something nobody controls unilaterally. Otherwise you're just trusting the company that trained the model, and that's the situation we have today.

And I think the long-term consequence is interesting. If people are rewarded for data, you change who shows up to contribute. Experts, communities with specialized knowledge, people in languages that are underrepresented today, they suddenly have a reason to participate. So it's not only about fairness, it's about getting better models, because the incentives finally point toward the data that's actually missing.

r001.rationale: The response says contributors receive tokens when a model is trained, allocated in proportion to their contributions, and describes the token as specific to that model.

r002.rationale: It proposes sending a portion of inference revenue to token holders whenever the model is used, for as long as the model remains useful.

astra-6.text:
I think the idea is that if you contribute data that makes a model more useful, you should participate in the value that model creates. So a model could have its own token, and some of those tokens would go to the people contributing training data, alongside the people contributing compute and doing the work to build it.

The hard part is figuring out how much a particular contribution is worth. You don’t want to reward somebody just for uploading a huge amount of data. A small amount of really valuable, unique data could improve the model much more. And the value depends on what the model already knows—something that’s useful for one model might add very little to another.

So I’d think of the token as a way to align those participants around making the model better. But you still need a mechanism to evaluate contributions. Issuing a token doesn’t, by itself, solve that attribution problem.

r001.rationale: The response says a model could have its own token and that some tokens would go to people contributing training data.

r002.rationale: It discusses sharing value and allocating tokens, but does not propose distributing the model’s revenue to token holders throughout the model’s lifetime.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the idea is that if you contribute data that makes a model more useful, you should share in the value that model creates. A model-specific token could represent that participation, so as people pay to use the model, some of that revenue goes back to the people who helped train it.

The hard part is figuring out how much each contribution actually helped. You don’t want to reward somebody simply for uploading a lot of data. You want to reward useful information, diversity, or expertise that the model was missing. And that’s a difficult attribution problem, because the value often comes from many contributions working together.

So I would think of the token as a way to align incentives, but you still need a credible way to evaluate contributions. Otherwise, you’re incentivizing people to produce more data rather than better data.

r001.rationale: It proposes a model-specific token to represent contributors’ participation in the value created by the model they helped train.

r002.rationale: It says some revenue would go back to contributors as people pay to use the model, but does not specify distribution to token holders throughout the model’s lifetime.
